CausalChain: Dietary and environmental factors → Alterations in gut microbiota composition → Enhanced microbial conversion of primary bile acids into tumor‐suppressive metabolites like UDCA and reduced formation of pro‐inflammatory secondary bile acids (e.g. DCA, LCA) → Selective activation of nuclear receptors (FXR, VDR) over pro‐inflammatory receptors (TGR5) → Attenuation of NF‐κB and MAPK signaling → Reduced epithelial–mesenchymal transition and proliferation in tumor cells
Hypothesis: Modulating the gut microbiota through dietary or probiotic interventions can shift the bile acid pool toward a more tumor suppressive composition (increasing UDCA relative to DCA/LCA), thereby reprogramming bile acid receptor signaling to reduce pro-inflammatory and proliferative pathways in cancers such as colorectal and esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that bile acids play a dual role in carcinogenesis, with effects that vary depending on their chemical structure, concentration, receptor activation, and derivation through microbial transformation. Notably, bile acids such as deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA) have been associated with pro‐carcinogenic signaling, whereas ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has been linked to tumor suppressive effects. Given the dynamic cross‐talk between host bile acid metabolism and the gut microbiota, we propose that intentional modulation of the microbiome to enrich beneficial bile acid conversions may shift the bile acid pool toward a tumor‐suppressive profile. This biological strategy might selectively activate favorable nuclear and membrane receptor pathways (for instance, activation of FXR and vitamin D receptor rather than overactivation of TGR5 in a pro‐inflammatory context) and thereby attenuate tumor progression in certain cancers such as colorectal or esophageal adenocarcinoma.
